title: Big stick to tame Big Tech
full_text:
Online platforms will have to protect their under-18 users from misogynistic content, pro-eating disorder material, bullying, pornography and crime glorification under proposed landmark laws.
The digital duty of care would complement the social media ban, meaning companies breaching the age laws would face a combined fine of more than $200m.
The draft laws released on Tuesday for consultation pave the way for Australians to have a choice between social media algorithms or a following-only feed, with platforms to be required to send users a pop-up asking them what they want as their “primary feed”.
All online platforms – including social media, AI chatbots and search engines – would have to protect all Australians from criminal content including child abuse, sexual violence, support for terrorist groups, encouraging suicide, and illicit drug use.
Additional protections would need to be in place for children and the minister would be able to add new categories of harm to both cohorts by regulation.
The laws, to be introduced to parliament next month, would also give the eSafety Commissioner the power to order nudify apps or websites down.
The government’s beefed-up social media ban is meanwhile set to pass the Senate this week, which will make failure to comply with an eSafety summons for interrogation punishable by up to 12 months imprisonment.
Communications Minister Anika Wells said there was a “global reckoning” coming for Big Tech that “started here in Australia”.
“It started with our world-leading social media minimum age laws. With our digital duty of care, we are taking the next step forward,” she said.
“Australia is setting basic safety standards … tech standards can still move fast, but they will no longer be allowed to break things.” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the duty of care was ”not about giving government control, it’s about giving people control”.
“We have an opportunity to shape technology for the better, rather than let it shape us,” he said.
Emma Mason, who spearheaded News Corp’s Let Them Be Kids campaign after losing her daughter Tilly to suicide, said the two laws will go “hand-in-hand”.
“They sit together, and that’s what’s needed,” she said.
Fellow parent advocate Wayne Holdsworth, whose son Mac died by suicide, said without the law, the atrocities that would continue “will be equivalent to (what) occurred through World War II”.
“We have an opportunity to mitigate that risk,” he said.
Opposition communications spokeswoman Sarah Henderson said the draft duty of care laws “raise serious free speech concerns”, while One Nation leader Pauline Hanson accused Labor of “copying the Chinese Communist Party’s censorship playbook”.
The Coalition will oppose Labor’s push to give eSafety compulsory interrogation powers, with Senator Henderson labelling them “coercive”. james morrow p13
